items.text: The analytical approach of selecting representative conflicts and applying a consistent framework (cause, legal basis, means, outcome, long-term consequence) rather than cataloguing every intervention.
Select 3–4 representative cases and use the same analytical framework for each: why intervene, legal/political basis, means used, outcome, cost, long-term consequence.
Do not list wars without evaluating goals and outcomes.
Do not assume every U.S. intervention had the same legal basis.
Do not equate battlefield victory with long-term political success.
The Korean War (1950–53) was fought under UN command; the Gulf War (1991) had explicit UN Security Council authorisation.
Vietnam and the post-2001 Afghanistan/Iraq wars each demonstrated the limits of converting military capability into durable political success.
Use a consistent analytical framework (cause, legal basis, means, outcome, consequence) across a small number of case studies, rather than attempting comprehensive coverage.
Legal and political bases for U.S. intervention varied significantly across cases (UN authorisation, NATO framework, unilateral action) — never assume uniformity.
